posts.cooked:
I don't see the point in playing a reveal-cards-and-decide type card unless you're going to use that info to help the group. Part of the fun is in planning what you can do together. We often have little discussions about which card to put on top and which on the bottom, taking into consideration what everyone's planning to do this turn and what cards they have. There seems to be an unwritten consensus that the person who played the card gets the final decision but the other players definitely have input. 

Think about it in terms of a solo game where you're playing three heroes. If you know a particular card's coming up you'll respond to that with every hero you control, because it's impossible to un-know that information. A three-player, three-hero game should be no different.

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked:
Okay, crossed wire there.  I meant Old Ben.

The game is cooperative in that the players are all working toward the same goal.  That doesn't mean that their ability to coordinate their efforts ought to be perfect.  Would Lord of the Rings have been a better story if Frodo and Sam and Merry and Aragorn had all had magic radios that let them talk to each other constantly across any distance?  Don't spy thrillers set in the modern day, where everyone does have a radio, periodically have the heroes unable to get a signal for some technical reason, specifically because the story requires that they be out of touch?

A game is a bit different than a story, but they both have a goal which is not always ideally served by making everything easy.  The goal of the story is to entertain, and making the characters' lives difficult can create more drama.  The goal of the game is to be engaging, and rules that impede player success can make for a more meaningful challenge.

posts.cooked:
I agree with Silverleaf.  If this were a movie, yeah...foreknowledge would spoil a lot of the drama inherent to one team member learning that "Oh, no!  My allies are about to walk into a trap!"  But, this isn't a movie and narrative tropes don't really apply here.

In the context of the game, the heroes are supposed to use every advantage at their disposal to defeat the villain.  The biggest piece of that arsenal is the use of human intelligence, as opposed to the Villain and Environment decks, which run pretty much automatically.  Sharing information falls into the purview of human intelligence.

Beyond that, this is a game that has a finite "win" and "loss" condition.  Either you defeat the villain or you don't.  The goal isn't to "play the game in an engaging manner" but rather to "help the team defeat the villain".  Where an RPG can still be interesting or even fun when the heroes lose, as a loss provides interesting plot points to hang new stories on, there's nothing beyond the single game of Sentinels (barring continual campaign-based SotM games, which are certainly not the norm).  In seeking a more desirable "win" over the "loss", sharing information is always a better idea than not.

For what it's worth, my group does use "closed" hands most times (though we do have players that play with "open" hands--it's personal preference, really).  However, we often ask or say things like "Is someone able to take care of that Ongoing this turn?" or "Hey, focus your damage on the big bad--I've got the minions this round."  And, anytime we reveal a villain or environment card, those get shared with the group.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
I love this game, but simply as mechanics you can do a lot better.

Sentinels shines because the mechanics are good, the cards are attractive and the characters are engaging.

I don't play the game to tell a story, but to fight as Fanatic or Visionary or Expat etc.  The decks do a great job of giving us the character and personality of these heroes, and integrating that into my playing of the game is a big part of why I love this game.

Nothing is ever "just a game," Silverleaf has already said that she doesn't play solo, so the group experience is important for her, others try to kill off every hero they can while still winning, some go for high scores and some for the most difficult matches they can get into.  Everyone takes more away from the experience than just the game itself having been played.  That's why we love it.

There isn't one way to play.  Each game is the domain of the group playing it.
